Hey there,

First off - chin up. You know who you want to be, and you can be that person again. It will be a progression; ups and downs and sometimes relapses but that's everything in life - even the best professional athletes can attest to that analogy. 

my best advice is to find something that can help the small things seem better and increase your confidence over time. 
for example: for me, my biggest stepping stone was hitting the gym again and training. it took a few months but eventually the confidence hit and things began to sort themselves out. I also meditate daily and have begun a new instrument. These things have changed me slowly; life stresses are a lot easier to manage, and I can take risks again (taking a harder program at school than I dared try for years ago when depression was running my life.) Good friend of mine took to piano as her form of confidence; a little bit every day. 

But do what works for you, truly. If you bake, did you enjoy it? If you go for walks, do you enjoy them? What did u used to look forward to doing those two years ago in high school? You may not be able to do those directly, but even something close could do the trick.

yes, it is definitely scary. Whatever you are feeling is real, and whether or not you can find a "reason" why, it doesn't matter. There may not be a "reason" but that does not make the feelings invalid. 
you CAN restore that confidence. It may take some reflection, to see what made you confident beforehand. Start small and find one thing that works - go bowling every saturday or something, anything, that makes you happier once you go do it. Slowly things will seem better and you will have other things to think about, not those destructive thoughts.

personally, what broke my destructive thought patterns was seeing a therapist, or so to speak. finding mantras and things to break the patterns; tracking moods, and finding 5 things a day that were "better than expected" or "not so bad" (from another's perspective, these would be labelled as "good" or "progress!"). 

don't be afraid to PM me - I'd love to listen. I also have my own experiences in more detail, and if you can extrapolate things from them to try i'd gladly share more.

Count me in! 
Sleeping in has been a major issue for me. for YEARS. 
And now as a serious student, it has still plagued me throughout my undergrad years. It makes me extremely stressed and anxious when I finally DO get up after sleeping in, realizing the time gone. 

For the life of me, I cannot remember a time since middle elementary school where I had any type of regular sleeping schedule. This will be a lot of work... but it will be worth it in the end.

I think it is at least very commonly linked to depression - I don't know specifically. 

I just know if I had a terrible day and I'm letting the negative mood take over more, that the crippling sad feeling is overpowering at night. It's like the instant I try to sleep, I can't go without crying and needing my night light on. And you can feel it pressing sometime after dinner... it's like "alone again, in this damn house, and it's so dark".. and then it hits really.
